cards.front: If you are asked to draw a plan, where do you look from?
cards.back: From directly above.

options.explanation: A plan is the view obtained by looking vertically down at the solid from directly above, showing its width and depth but not its height.
Looking from below would produce an underside view, not a plan. A plan is drawn by looking directly down at the solid from above.
Looking directly in front produces a front elevation, which shows width and height. A plan is obtained by looking directly from above.
Looking directly beside the solid produces a side elevation, showing depth and height. A plan is drawn from the view directly above.

cards.front: If you draw the front elevation, where do you look from?
cards.back: From the front.

options.explanation: A front elevation is the two-dimensional view seen when looking straight at the designated front of the solid, showing its width and height.
Looking from the back gives a rear elevation, which may differ from the front view. The front elevation is obtained by looking from the front.
Looking from above produces the plan, which shows width and depth. The front elevation is drawn by looking straight at the solid from the front.
Looking from the side produces a side elevation, usually showing depth and height. A front elevation must be viewed from the solid’s front.

cards.front: For a side elevation, how do you choose the side to view?
cards.back: Use the side shown by the arrow or label.

options.text: Use the side shown by the arrow or label.
options.explanation: The diagram’s arrow or label identifies the required viewing direction, so the side elevation must be drawn as seen from that specified side.

options.text: Use the side opposite the arrow or label.
options.explanation: Reversing the indicated direction produces the elevation from the opposite side. The required side is the one shown by the arrow or label.

options.text: Use the side with the longest visible edge.
options.explanation: The lengths of the edges do not determine the viewing side. The correct side elevation is selected using the arrow or label on the diagram.

options.text: Use the side nearest to the front of the page.
options.explanation: The position of a side on the printed page does not determine the required view. Follow the arrow or label that specifies the viewing side.

cards.front: Width is [ ___ ]; depth is [ ___ ].
cards.back: Width is left-to-right; depth is front-to-back.

options.text: Width is left-to-right; depth is front-to-back.
options.explanation: Width measures the horizontal distance from left to right, while depth measures how far the solid extends from its front to its back.

options.text: Width is front-to-back; depth is left-to-right.
options.explanation: This swaps the meanings of width and depth. Width runs left-to-right, while depth runs front-to-back when describing the dimensions of a solid.

options.text: Width is bottom-to-top; depth is front-to-back.
options.explanation: Bottom-to-top is height, not width. Width runs left-to-right, while the stated front-to-back direction for depth is correct.

options.text: Width is left-to-right; depth is bottom-to-top.
options.explanation: Bottom-to-top describes height rather than depth. Width runs left-to-right, and depth measures the front-to-back distance of the solid.

cards.front: A length is measured bottom-to-top on a solid. Which measurement is this?
cards.back: Height.

options.explanation: Height is the vertical measurement of a solid, taken from its bottom to its top. It is visible in front and side elevations.
Width measures from left to right rather than bottom to top. A bottom-to-top measurement is the solid’s height.
Depth measures the distance from front to back, not the vertical distance. The bottom-to-top dimension of a solid is its height.
Length is a general term and usually refers to a horizontal extent in this context. The named bottom-to-top dimension is height.

cards.front: Which dimension is not shown in a plan?
cards.back: Height.

options.explanation: A plan is viewed from above, so it shows the solid’s width and depth. Its vertical height cannot be seen in this view.
A plan shows the left-to-right width because it is viewed from above. Height is the dimension that is not shown.
A plan shows the front-to-back depth as well as the width. It does not show the solid’s bottom-to-top height.
Horizontal lengths form the outline visible in a plan, so they can be shown. The missing dimension is the vertical height.

cards.front: Which dimension is not shown in a front elevation?
cards.back: Depth.

options.explanation: A front elevation shows the solid’s left-to-right width and bottom-to-top height. It cannot show the full front-to-back depth.
Height is visible in a front elevation as the bottom-to-top measurement. The dimension not shown is the front-to-back depth.
Width is visible in a front elevation as the left-to-right measurement. The front-to-back depth is the dimension that is not shown.
A front elevation specifically displays both width and height. It leaves out the third dimension, which is the solid’s depth.

cards.front: Which full measurement does a side elevation not show?
cards.back: The left-to-right width.

options.explanation: A side elevation shows the solid’s depth and height. Looking from the side means the full left-to-right width extends along the viewing direction and is not shown.
A side elevation shows the front-to-back depth as a horizontal measurement. The dimension it does not show is the solid’s left-to-right width.
A side elevation shows the bottom-to-top height as its vertical measurement. The hidden full dimension is the left-to-right width.
Front-to-back is depth, not width, and this distance is visible in a side elevation. The unshown dimension is the left-to-right width.

cards.front: The plan and front elevation share the [ ___ ].
cards.back: The plan and front elevation share the width.

options.explanation: Both views show the solid’s left-to-right measurement, so the plan and front elevation must have the same width.
Height is visible in the front elevation but not in the plan. The shared dimension is width because both views show the left-to-right measurement.
Depth is shown by the plan but not by the front elevation. These two views instead share the solid’s width.
Length is sometimes used informally for a horizontal measurement, but the corresponding dimension in the plan and front elevation is specifically called width.

cards.front: The plan and side elevation share the [ ___ ].
cards.back: The plan and side elevation share the depth.

options.explanation: Both the plan and side elevation show the solid’s front-to-back measurement, so their shared dimension is depth.
Width is shared by the plan and front elevation, not the plan and side elevation. The plan and side elevation both show depth.
Height appears in the side elevation but is not represented in the plan. The dimension common to these two views is depth.
Length may be used informally for a horizontal dimension, but plans and elevations specifically identify the shared front-to-back measurement as depth.

cards.front: The front elevation and side elevation share the [ ___ ].
cards.back: The front elevation and side elevation share the height.

options.explanation: Both elevations show the vertical measurement of the solid, so the front and side elevations share the same height.
Width is visible in the front elevation but not the side elevation. Both elevations instead share the solid’s vertical dimension, which is height.
Depth is visible in the side elevation but not the front elevation. The shared dimension between the two elevations is height.
Length may describe a horizontal dimension, whereas the dimension common to both the front and side elevations is the vertical height.

cards.front: If a solid is a prism, what happens to its cross-section through the solid?
cards.back: The same cross-section continues all the way through.

options.text: The same cross-section continues all the way through.
options.explanation: A prism has a uniform cross-section along its length, meaning the same cross-sectional shape and size continue from one end to the other.

options.text: The cross-section decreases all the way through.
options.explanation: A steadily shrinking cross-section describes a tapered solid, such as a pyramid or cone. A prism keeps the same cross-section all the way through.

options.text: The cross-section increases all the way through.
options.explanation: A steadily enlarging cross-section describes a widening or tapered solid, not a prism. A prism has the same cross-section throughout its length.

options.text: The cross-section rotates all the way through.
options.explanation: Rotation of the cross-section would produce a twisted solid rather than an ordinary prism. In a prism, the same cross-section continues straight through.

cards.front: For a cube solid, what positions should be marked on the plan?
cards.back: Every floor square with at least one cube.

options.text: Every floor square with at least one cube.
options.explanation: A plan is a view from directly above, so each floor position occupied by one or more cubes appears as a square.

options.text: Every floor square with exactly one cube.
options.explanation: Marking only positions with exactly one cube ignores taller stacks, although they still occupy floor space. Every position containing at least one cube must be shown.

options.text: Every floor square with at least two cubes.
options.explanation: Requiring at least two cubes wrongly omits single cubes. From above, any occupied floor square is shown, regardless of the stack’s height.

options.text: Every floor square with no cubes present.
options.explanation: Empty floor positions are not part of the solid and therefore do not appear in its plan. Only squares with at least one cube are marked.

cards.front: A tower is 3 cubes high. How many squares does it show in the plan?
cards.back: One square.

options.explanation: The plan records occupied floor positions rather than the number of cubes in a stack. One vertical tower therefore appears as one square.
Counting three squares confuses the tower’s height with its footprint. All three cubes occupy the same floor position, so the plan shows one square.
Two squares would imply two occupied floor positions. A single vertical tower occupies only one position, so its plan contains one square.
Six squares may come from counting visible cube faces rather than the footprint. A plan shows occupied floor positions, so this tower gives one square.

cards.front: In a cube-solid side elevation, what height is drawn at each depth position?
cards.back: The maximum stack height at that depth.

options.text: The maximum stack height at that depth.
options.explanation: Looking from the side combines stacks that share a depth position, so the visible outline reaches the greatest stack height found there.

options.text: The minimum stack height at that depth.
options.explanation: Using the minimum height ignores taller stacks that block shorter ones in the side view. The elevation must show the maximum stack height at each depth.

options.text: The total stack height at that depth.
options.explanation: Adding stack heights counts cubes hidden behind one another rather than forming the visible outline. The side elevation uses only the maximum height at each depth.

options.text: The average stack height at that depth.
options.explanation: An average height does not represent the solid’s outline and could create a height no stack has. The maximum stack height must be drawn at each depth.

cards.front: A cylinder has a [ ___ ] plan and [ ___ ] elevations.
cards.back: A cylinder has a circular plan and rectangular elevations.

options.text: A cylinder has a circular plan and rectangular elevations.
options.explanation: Viewed from above, a vertical cylinder shows its circular base. From either horizontal direction, its curved surface projects as a rectangle.

options.text: A cylinder has a rectangular plan and circular elevations.
options.explanation: This reverses the two projections. A vertical cylinder appears circular from above in the plan and rectangular from the front or side.

options.text: A cylinder has a circular plan and circular elevations.
options.explanation: The plan is circular, but a horizontal view includes the cylinder’s height and diameter, producing a rectangular elevation rather than a circle.

options.text: A cylinder has a rectangular plan and rectangular elevations.
options.explanation: The elevations are rectangular, but the plan shows the cylinder’s circular base rather than a rectangle. Therefore only the plan should be circular.

cards.front: A cone has a [ ___ ] plan and [ ___ ] elevations.
cards.back: A cone has a circular plan and triangular elevations.

options.text: A cone has a circular plan and triangular elevations.
options.explanation: Viewed from above, the circular base determines the plan. Viewed from the side or front, the apex and base diameter form a triangular outline.

options.text: A cone has a square plan and triangular elevations.
options.explanation: A square plan would belong to an object with a square base, such as a square-based pyramid. A cone has a circular plan and triangular elevations.

options.text: A cone has a circular plan and rectangular elevations.
options.explanation: The circular plan is correct, but a rectangular elevation is associated with a cylinder. A cone narrows to an apex, so its elevations are triangular.

options.text: A cone has a triangular plan and circular elevations.
options.explanation: This reverses the shapes seen from above and from the side. A cone has a circular plan because of its base, while its elevations are triangular.

cards.front: A square-based pyramid has a [ ___ ] plan and [ ___ ] elevations.
cards.back: A square-based pyramid has a square plan and triangular elevations.

options.text: A square-based pyramid has a square plan and triangular elevations.
options.explanation: The view from above shows the square base, so the plan is square. From the front or side, the base and apex produce a triangular elevation.

options.text: A square-based pyramid has a rectangular plan and triangular elevations.
options.explanation: A rectangle is tempting because every square is a type of rectangle, but plans use the precise visible shape. The plan is square and the elevations are triangular.

options.text: A square-based pyramid has a square plan and rectangular elevations.
options.explanation: The plan is square, but rectangular elevations would not show the sides meeting at an apex. The sloping faces produce triangular elevations.

options.text: A square-based pyramid has a triangular plan and square elevations.
options.explanation: This confuses the base shape with the shape of a side view. The square base gives a square plan, while the apex creates triangular elevations.

cards.front: A cone has radius 2 cm. What is the base length in its side elevation?
cards.back: 4 cm.

options.explanation: The base in the side elevation is the cone’s diameter. Since the diameter is twice the radius, its length is $2 \times 2 = 4$ cm.
This uses the radius as the full base length. The side elevation shows the diameter, so the correct base length is $2 \times 2 = 4$ cm.
This calculates the circumference using $2\pi r$, but the side elevation needs the straight-line diameter. Doubling the radius gives the correct base length of 4 cm.
This doubles the diameter after already doubling the radius. The base spans one diameter only, so $2 \times 2$ gives the correct length of 4 cm.

cards.front: Where should the apex go in a cone side elevation?
cards.back: Directly above the midpoint of the base.

options.text: Directly above the midpoint of the base.
options.explanation: A right cone is symmetrical about its perpendicular axis. Therefore, its apex must be vertically aligned with the midpoint of the base in the side elevation.

options.text: Directly above the left endpoint of the base.
options.explanation: Placing the apex over an endpoint creates a skewed triangular outline rather than a symmetrical right cone. It should be directly above the midpoint of the base.

options.text: Directly above the right endpoint of the base.
options.explanation: Aligning the apex with the right endpoint incorrectly makes one side vertical and destroys the cone’s symmetry. The apex belongs above the midpoint of the base.

options.text: Directly above the quarter-point of the base.
options.explanation: The quarter-point does not lie on the cone’s central axis, so this placement would produce an asymmetrical elevation. The apex should be above the base midpoint.

cards.front: For a cone or pyramid elevation, which height is normally used?
cards.back: The perpendicular height.

options.explanation: An elevation uses the vertical distance from the base to the apex. This is the perpendicular height, measured at a right angle to the base.
The slant height runs along a face from the apex to the base edge, so it is not the vertical height normally used. Use the perpendicular height.
A cone has no vertical edge, and a pyramid’s edges are generally sloping. The required height is the perpendicular distance from the base to the apex.
The base length controls the width of the elevation rather than its height. The vertical dimension to the apex is given by the perpendicular height.

cards.front: Using a scale of 2 cm to 1 m, how long should 250 cm be drawn?
cards.back: 5 cm.

options.explanation: First convert 250 cm to 2.5 m. At 2 cm for each metre, the drawing length is $2.5 \times 2 = 5$ cm.
This converts 250 cm to 2.5 m but then treats each metre as only 1 cm. Multiplying by the stated 2 cm gives 5 cm.
This divides 2.5 m by the scale value instead of multiplying by 2 cm per metre. The correct drawing length is $2.5 \times 2 = 5$ cm.
This multiplies 250 by 2 without first converting centimetres to metres, mixing real and drawing units. Since 250 cm is 2.5 m, draw 5 cm.
